objectives.statement: Identify the composition of a nucleus, use proton number (Z) and nucleon number (A) to find the number of neutrons, write and interpret nuclide notation, and identify isotopes.
Relate proton number to the overall positive charge of a nucleus, and distinguish nuclear fission (a nucleus splitting) from nuclear fusion (nuclei joining).

theory_blocks.title: What is actually inside an atom
theory_blocks.body:
An atom is mostly empty space. Almost all of its mass is packed into a tiny central [[blue:**nucleus**]], built from two kinds of particle: **protons**, each with a relative charge of $+1$, and **neutrons**, with a relative charge of $0$ (no charge at all). Much lighter **electrons**, each with a relative charge of $-1$, exist at a relatively large distance from this nucleus.

Because a proton and an electron carry equal-sized opposite charges, a neutral atom (one with no overall charge) must have exactly as many electrons as it has protons. Nothing about the neutrons affects this balance, since neutrons carry no charge.

assets.caption: A simple model of a neutral atom (helium): a tiny, dense nucleus of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, with 2 much lighter electrons at a relatively large distance. The number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the atom has no overall charge. Not to scale.
assets.purpose: Make the scale and particle composition of an atom concrete before Z, A and neutrons are defined.

theory_blocks.title: Proton number, nucleon number and nuclide notation
theory_blocks.body:
Two counts fix exactly which nuclide (which specific type of nucleus) you are describing:

- The **proton number** (also called the atomic number), symbol $Z$, is the number of protons in the nucleus. It also fixes which element the atom is, since every atom of a given element has the same $Z$.
- The **nucleon number** (also called the mass number), symbol $A$, is the total number of protons **and** neutrons in the nucleus.

Since $A$ counts protons and neutrons together, the number of neutrons is found by:
$$N = A - Z$$

A nuclide is written in **nuclide notation** as $^{A}_{Z}X$, with the nucleon number above and the proton number below, immediately to the left of the chemical symbol $X$. For carbon-14, written $^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}$: $Z=6$ and $A=14$, so $N = 14-6=8$ neutrons. Check: $6+8=14$, which matches $A$.

theory_blocks.title: Isotopes: same element, different nucleon number
theory_blocks.body:
**Isotopes** are nuclides of the same element - so they share exactly the same proton number $Z$ - that have different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different nucleon numbers $A$.

Carbon-12 ($^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}$) and carbon-14 ($^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}$) are isotopes of carbon: both have $Z=6$, so both are definitely carbon, but carbon-12 has $12-6=6$ neutrons while carbon-14 has $14-6=8$ neutrons. Because the proton number is unchanged, both isotopes have identical chemical behaviour; only their mass, and in some cases their nuclear stability, differs. An element may have several isotopes, and some isotopes are **radioactive** (unstable): carbon-14 is radioactive, while carbon-12 is stable.

theory_blocks.title: A is not the number of electrons
theory_blocks.body: It is tempting to treat the nucleon number $A$ as a total count of 'everything in the atom', including electrons. It is not: $A$ only ever counts protons and neutrons, both of which live in the nucleus. [[blue:The number of electrons in a **neutral** atom equals $Z$, never $A$.]] For sodium-23 ($Z=11$, $A=23$): there are 11 electrons (equal to $Z$) and $23-11=12$ neutrons - and neither of those numbers is 23.

theory_blocks.title: Nuclear charge, fission and fusion
theory_blocks.body:
Since every proton carries one unit of positive charge and neutrons carry none, the overall relative charge of a nucleus is simply $+Z$: a nucleus with $Z=11$ has relative charge $+11$.

Two processes split or join whole nuclei:

- **Nuclear fission** is a large, heavy nucleus **splitting** into two smaller nuclei (usually with some neutrons released too). This is the process used in nuclear power stations.
- **Nuclear fusion** is two light nuclei **joining** to form one heavier nucleus. This is the process that powers the Sun, where hydrogen nuclei join to form helium.

Both change which element(s) are present, because splitting or joining nuclei changes the proton number - unlike a chemical reaction, which never touches the nucleus at all.

worked_examples.statement: **Oxygen-16.** An oxygen-16 nuclide has proton number $Z=8$ and nucleon number $A=16$. Find the number of neutrons it contains.
reasoning: Neutrons are found from $N=A-Z$, since $A$ already counts protons and neutrons together.
worked_examples.solution: $N = 16-8=8$ neutrons.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $8\text{ protons}+8\text{ neutrons}=16$, which matches the given nucleon number.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reading off 16 as the number of neutrons directly, instead of subtracting the proton number first.

worked_examples.statement: **Two isotopes of carbon.** Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have proton number $Z=6$. Find the number of neutrons in each, and state what is the same and what is different between them.
reasoning: Use $N=A-Z$ for each nuclide separately, since they have different nucleon numbers.
Compare the proton numbers (same) with the neutron numbers (different) to classify the pair.
worked_examples.solution: Carbon-12: $N=12-6=6$ neutrons. Carbon-14: $N=14-6=8$ neutrons.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both have $Z=6$, so both are carbon (same element, same chemistry); they differ only in neutron number (6 versus 8), which is exactly what makes them isotopes of each other.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding that because the neutron counts differ, the proton counts must differ too, and wrongly calling them different elements.

worked_examples.statement: **Are uranium-235 and uranium-238 isotopes of each other?** Uranium has proton number $Z=92$. Find the number of neutrons in uranium-235 and in uranium-238, and decide whether they are isotopes of each other.
reasoning: Find neutrons for each: $N=A-Z$.
Being isotopes only requires the *same* proton number; the neutron numbers are expected to differ.
worked_examples.solution: Uranium-235: $N=235-92=143$ neutrons. Uranium-238: $N=238-92=146$ neutrons. Since both have $Z=92$, they are isotopes of each other.
worked_examples.interpretation: The decision rests entirely on $Z$ being equal (both 92), not on the neutron counts being equal - they are deliberately different (143 versus 146).
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding they are not isotopes because the neutron numbers (143 and 146) are different, instead of checking the proton numbers first.

worked_examples.statement: **Writing a nuclide from a description.** A nucleus contains 92 protons and 143 neutrons. (a) Write its nucleon number and proton number. (b) Write it in nuclide notation, using the symbol U for this element. (c) State whether this nuclide is the same element as one with 92 protons and 146 neutrons.
unknowns: $A$, $Z$, nuclide notation, and whether the second nuclide is the same element
reasoning: Proton number $Z$ is simply the number of protons given.
Nucleon number $A$ is protons plus neutrons added together.
Two nuclides are the same element exactly when their proton numbers match, regardless of neutron number.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $Z=92$, $A=92+143=235$. (b) $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}$. (c) Yes: the second nuclide also has $Z=92$ (since $92$ protons is unchanged), so it is the same element, uranium - specifically the isotope uranium-238, since $92+146=238$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Part (c) is answered purely from matching proton numbers; the different neutron count (143 versus 146) only tells you they are different isotopes of the same element, not different elements.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Adding protons and neutrons in the wrong order when writing nuclide notation, or placing $Z$ above and $A$ below instead of $A$ above and $Z$ below.

worked_examples.statement: **Fission or fusion?** (a) In a nuclear power station, a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing more neutrons. (b) In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei join together, in several steps, to form helium nuclei. Identify each process and justify your answer using the words 'split' or 'join'.
knowns: (a) one large nucleus becomes two smaller nuclei
(b) light nuclei join to become a heavier nucleus
reasoning: Fission is defined by a nucleus splitting into smaller pieces.
Fusion is defined by nuclei joining to form a single, heavier nucleus.
worked_examples.solution: (a) This is **nuclear fission**: one large uranium nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei. (b) This is **nuclear fusion**: light hydrogen nuclei join to form heavier helium nuclei.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both processes change the proton number of the nuclei involved and therefore change which element(s) are present - this is a nuclear change, never a chemical one, however similar the word 'reaction' might sound.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calling the power-station process 'fusion' because it 'produces energy', instead of checking whether nuclei are splitting (fission) or joining (fusion).

guided_exercises.statement: A fluorine nuclide has proton number $Z=9$ and nucleon number $A=19$. Find the number of neutrons, and check your answer.
hints: Identify which number is $A$ and which is $Z$ from the statement.
Use $N=A-Z$.
Check by adding your neutron count back to $Z$ and confirming you recover $A$.
common_errors: Subtracting the numbers in the wrong order and reporting a negative or nonsensical result.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify which number is $A$ and which is $Z$ from the statement.

**Step 2 — Method:** Use $N=A-Z$.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $N=19-9=10$ neutrons. Check: $9+10=19$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check by adding your neutron count back to $Z$ and confirming you recover $A$.

guided_exercises.statement: Nuclide X has $Z=17$ and $A=35$. Nuclide Y has $Z=17$ and $A=37$. State whether X and Y are isotopes of each other, and justify your answer.
hints: Compare the proton numbers of X and Y first.
Remember that isotopes require the *same* proton number.
The nucleon numbers are allowed - and expected - to differ.
guided_exercises.answer: Yes, X and Y are isotopes of each other, because they share the same proton number ($Z=17$ for both) and differ only in nucleon number (35 versus 37), meaning they differ only in neutron number.
common_errors: Saying they are not isotopes because $A$ differs, without checking that $Z$ is actually the same for both.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Compare the proton numbers of X and Y first.

**Step 2 — Method:** Remember that isotopes require the *same* proton number.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Yes, X and Y are isotopes of each other, because they share the same proton number ($Z=17$ for both) and differ only in nucleon number (35 versus 37), meaning they differ only in neutron number.

**Step 4 — Check:** The nucleon numbers are allowed - and expected - to differ.

exercises.statement: A nitrogen-14 nuclide has proton number $Z=7$ and nucleon number $A=14$. Find the number of neutrons.
exercises.answer: $N=14-7=7$ neutrons.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $7+7=14$, matching the given nucleon number.

exercises.statement: Potassium-39 and potassium-40 both have proton number $Z=19$. Find the number of neutrons in each, and state whether they are isotopes of each other.
exercises.answer: Potassium-39: $N=39-19=20$ neutrons. Potassium-40: $N=40-19=21$ neutrons. They are isotopes of each other, since both have $Z=19$.

exercises.statement: A nucleus contains 20 protons and 20 neutrons, and this element's symbol is Ca. Write its nucleon number, proton number and full nuclide notation.
exercises.answer: $Z=20$, $A=20+20=40$, nuclide notation $^{40}_{20}\mathrm{Ca}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: protons plus neutrons, $20+20=40$, matches $A$.

exercises.statement: A nuclear reactor splits uranium nuclei to release energy; the Sun joins hydrogen nuclei to release energy. Identify each process, and explain, using the words 'split' and 'join', why these are nuclear processes rather than chemical reactions, even though chemical reactions can also release energy.
exercises.answer: The reactor process is nuclear fission (a nucleus splits into smaller nuclei); the Sun's process is nuclear fusion (nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus). Both are nuclear, not chemical, because the change happens inside the nucleus itself (changing the proton number and so the element), whereas a chemical reaction only ever rearranges electrons between atoms and never changes any nucleus.
exercises.full_solution: Releasing energy is not, by itself, evidence of a nuclear process - chemical reactions release energy too. The decisive evidence is that the nucleus changes.

exam_questions.statement: A lithium nuclide is written $^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$. (a) State its number of protons, neutrons and electrons, assuming the atom is neutral. (b) A second lithium nuclide, $^{6}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$, exists. Explain why this is an isotope of the first nuclide.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Protons $=3$; neutrons $=7-3=4$; electrons $=3$ (equal to the proton number, since the atom is neutral). (b) $^{6}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$ is an isotope of $^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$ because both have the same proton number ($Z=3$, so both are lithium), but different nucleon numbers (6 versus 7), meaning different neutron counts (3 versus 4).
exam_questions.full_solution: Check: $3+4=7$ for the first nuclide, and $3+3=6$ for the second.
mark_scheme: States 3 protons.
States 4 neutrons, correctly calculated as $7-3$.
States 3 electrons, correctly linked to the proton number for a neutral atom.
Correctly explains the isotope relationship using matching $Z$ and differing $A$/neutron number.
common_errors: Giving 7 electrons by confusing $A$ with the electron count.

exam_questions.statement: (a) Define nuclear fission. (b) A nucleus with proton number 92 undergoes fission, splitting into two smaller nuclei (with some neutrons also released). State what happens to the total number of protons shared between the two smaller nuclei, compared with the original nucleus. (c) State one difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Nuclear fission is a large, heavy nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei. (b) The total number of protons shared between the two smaller nuclei is still 92 in total; no protons are created or destroyed, only redistributed between the two new nuclei. (c) Fission splits one large nucleus into smaller ones, while fusion joins two light nuclei into one heavier nucleus.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Nuclear fission is a large, heavy nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei. (b) The total number of protons shared between the two smaller nuclei is still 92 in total; no protons are created or destroyed, only redistributed between the two new nuclei. (c) Fission splits one large nucleus into smaller ones, while fusion joins two light nuclei into one heavier nucleus.
mark_scheme: Correctly defines fission as a large nucleus splitting into smaller nuclei.
States that the total proton number is conserved (stays at 92 in total across the products).
Links this to protons being neither created nor destroyed in the split.
Correctly states a valid difference between fission and fusion (splitting versus joining).
Expresses the difference clearly, naming both processes correctly.
common_errors: Describing fission and fusion with the directions swapped (saying fission joins nuclei).

mcq.stem: What does the nucleon number $A$ of a nuclide actually count?

options.text: The number of protons only.
options.why_wrong: this is what the proton number $Z$ counts, not $A$.

options.text: The number of protons plus the number of neutrons.
The number of electrons only.
options.why_wrong: electrons are not counted by $A$ at all; in a neutral atom their number equals $Z$, not $A$.

options.text: The number of neutrons only.
options.why_wrong: this is the neutron number, $N=A-Z$, which is only part of what $A$ counts.

mcq.explanation: $A$ is defined as protons plus neutrons together; neither alone, and never electrons.

mcq.stem: A carbon-14 nuclide has proton number $Z=6$. How many neutrons does it contain?

options.why_wrong: repeats the proton number instead of subtracting it from the nucleon number.
repeats the nucleon number $A$ directly, without subtracting $Z$ at all.
adds $Z$ and $A$ together ($6+14$) instead of subtracting.

mcq.explanation: Neutrons $=A-Z=14-6=8$.

mcq.stem: Two nuclides are isotopes of each other. What must be true of them?

options.text: They have the same nucleon number but a different proton number.
options.why_wrong: a different proton number means a different element, so these would not be isotopes of each other at all.

options.text: They have a different proton number but the same number of neutrons.
options.why_wrong: a different proton number again makes them different elements, not isotopes of one another.

options.text: They have the same number of electrons as each other but a different proton number from each other.
options.why_wrong: a neutral atom's electrons equal its proton number, so a different proton number would mean a different electron count too - and, again, a different element.

options.text: They have the same proton number but a different nucleon number.

mcq.explanation: Isotopes are defined by sharing the same proton number $Z$ (same element) while differing in nucleon number $A$ (different neutron count).

mcq.stem: Which of these is an example of nuclear fusion?

options.text: Two light hydrogen nuclei joining to form one heavier nucleus.
A large uranium nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei.
options.why_wrong: this describes nuclear fission, the opposite process.

options.text: A nucleus emitting a particle as it decays.
options.why_wrong: this describes radioactive decay, not nuclei splitting or joining as fission/fusion does.

options.text: An atom losing an electron to become a charged ion.
options.why_wrong: ionisation only involves electrons leaving the atom; it never involves the nucleus at all.

mcq.explanation: Fusion is defined as two (or more) light nuclei joining to form a single, heavier nucleus.

flashcards.front: What does the proton number $Z$ of a nucleus tell you?
flashcards.back: The number of protons it contains, which also fixes which element the atom is.

flashcards.front: What is the nucleon number $A$?
flashcards.back: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

flashcards.front: How do you find the number of neutrons from $Z$ and $A$?
flashcards.back: Neutrons $N = A - Z$.

flashcards.front: Does the nucleon number $A$ tell you how many electrons a neutral atom has?
flashcards.back: No. $A$ is protons plus neutrons only. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the proton number $Z$, not $A$.

flashcards.front: How are nuclear fission and nuclear fusion different?
flashcards.back: Fission splits one large nucleus into two smaller nuclei; fusion joins two light nuclei into one heavier nucleus. Both are nuclear changes, never chemical ones.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Two isotopes of the same element differ in the number of protons they contain.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Isotopes clearly differ in mass, and protons are the first particle count students learn about an element, so a mass difference is wrongly assigned to a proton difference.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: A learner changes Z when asked to write a second isotope of a given element.
misconceptions.correct_model: Isotopes of the same element share exactly the same proton number (Z) - that is what keeps them the same element - and differ only in the number of neutrons, which changes their nucleon number (A).
misconceptions.remediation: Place carbon-12 and carbon-14 side by side: show both have Z = 6 (so both are carbon), then show the neutron counts differ (6 and 8) and that this difference, not a proton difference, is what makes them different isotopes.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The nucleon number A counts the number of electrons in the atom.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A is usually the larger number printed next to the symbol, and before electrons are tied specifically to Z, it is tempting to attach the biggest number to 'how many particles the atom has altogether'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: A learner states that a sodium-23 atom has 23 electrons.
misconceptions.correct_model: A counts protons plus neutrons in the nucleus only, and says nothing directly about electrons. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the proton number Z, not A.
misconceptions.remediation: Take sodium-23 (Z = 11): confirm 11 electrons (equal to Z, since the atom is neutral) and 12 neutrons (since $23-11=12$), and note that neither of these equals 23.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Fission and fusion are chemical changes, because they produce a new substance.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both processes end with a different element present, which sounds exactly like what a chemical reaction does, and the vocabulary ('reaction', 'change') overlaps.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: A learner describes fission or fusion using chemical-bond language, such as 'the atoms rearrange their electrons'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Fission and fusion are nuclear changes: they alter the nucleus itself (splitting it apart or joining nuclei together), which changes the proton number and therefore the element. A chemical change only rearranges electrons between atoms and never touches any nucleus.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast directly: burning (chemical) leaves every nucleus involved completely unchanged, while fission or fusion changes which element is present because the nucleus itself has split or joined.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the nucleon number $A$ as the number of electrons.
common_mistakes.why: $A$ is usually the larger, more prominent number, which is easy to mistake for 'how many particles the atom has altogether'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Electrons in a neutral atom always equal $Z$, never $A$; always check which symbol a question is actually asking about.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming two nuclides with the same $A$ must be isotopes of each other.
common_mistakes.why: Isotopes are about belonging to the same element, and a matching number can look convincing even when it is the wrong number that matches.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Isotopes always share the same $Z$ (proton number); check $Z$ first, never $A$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing fission or fusion as a chemical change.
common_mistakes.why: Both processes end with a 'new substance' present, which sounds like what a chemical reaction does.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask whether the nucleus itself changed. If protons were gained, lost or rearranged inside the nucleus, the change is nuclear, not chemical.

exam_notes: State both the proton number and the nucleon number explicitly when describing a nuclide; a bare neutron count with no working rarely earns full marks.
When two nuclides are given, check their proton numbers first to decide whether they are isotopes; do not rely on how similar the nucleon numbers look.
Describe fission as a nucleus splitting and fusion as nuclei joining, in your own words - a vague phrase like 'a nuclear reaction happens' does not show which process is meant.

summary.big_idea: A nucleus is identified completely by its proton number and nucleon number; isotopes share the first but not the second, and splitting or joining nuclei (fission or fusion) is a nuclear change, never a chemical one.
key_points: Proton number $Z$ fixes the element; nucleon number $A$ counts protons plus neutrons together.
Neutrons are found from $N=A-Z$.
Isotopes share the same $Z$ but have different $A$ (different neutron counts).
In a neutral atom, electrons equal $Z$, never $A$.
Fission splits a large nucleus; fusion joins light nuclei - both change the element present, unlike any chemical reaction.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Compare proton numbers first: matching $Z$ means isotopes of the same element; a different $Z$ means a different element altogether.

02_Detecting_ionising_radiation.json.title: Detecting ionising radiation
02_Detecting_ionising_radiation.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Define ionising and background radiation, name the principal sources of background radiation, describe how a detector and counter record nuclear events, and calculate count rate using consistent units.

prerequisites.statement: State that an atom can lose or gain electrons to become a charged ion (an earlier lesson's nucleus/electron picture, carried forward).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Ionising radiation is defined by its ability to knock electrons out of atoms, so 'ion' needs to already mean something before this lesson can define it.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate a rate as a quantity divided by a time interval.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Count rate is exactly this kind of rate - counts divided by time - so the same per-unit-time thinking from earlier in the course applies directly, with no new structure to learn.

theory_blocks.title: A detector that 'hears' invisible events
theory_blocks.body:
Ionising radiation cannot be seen, heard or felt directly, yet a detector such as a Geiger-Muller tube can register each individual ionising event as it happens. Each time radiation passes through the tube and ionises the gas inside it, the tube produces a tiny electrical pulse, which a connected [[blue:**counter** registers as one **count**]] - often heard as a single click through a loudspeaker.

The counter does not know, and does not need to know, exactly what produced any one click. It simply adds up how many ionising events have been detected.

theory_blocks.title: Background radiation: the reading before a source is even introduced
Count rate: counts divided by time
theory_blocks.body:
A plain count on its own (for example, '30 counts') says nothing about how active a source is, because it depends on how long you measured for. The useful quantity is the **count rate**:
$$\text{count rate} = \dfrac{\text{number of counts}}{\text{time interval}}$$
measured in counts per second or counts per minute. For example, 30 counts recorded in 10 s gives a count rate of $30\div10=3$ counts per second. Two readings can only be compared fairly once both have been converted to the same rate unit, measured over the same kind of time interval.

theory_blocks.title: Making a fair comparison, and isolating the source
theory_blocks.body:
To find the count rate due to a sample alone, two separate measurements are needed, taken under identical conditions:

1. Measure the count rate with **no** sample present (the background count rate), at a fixed distance from the detector and over a chosen time interval.
2. Measure the count rate with the sample present, at the **same** distance and over an **equal** time interval.
3. Subtract: $\text{count rate due to sample} = \text{count rate with sample} - \text{background count rate}$.

Keeping the distance identical between the two measurements matters, because moving the detector closer or further away would change the count rate for reasons that have nothing to do with the sample itself. Counting for an equal time means the two raw counts can be compared directly; if the times differ, each count must first be divided by its own time to give a count rate before subtracting.

assets.caption: A source and a Geiger-Muller detector set up at a fixed, known distance $d$, connected to a counter that displays counts over a chosen time interval.
assets.purpose: Make explicit which quantities (distance, time) must be held the same between the background reading and the with-sample reading.

theory_blocks.title: Ionising radiation is invisible, and background is never exactly zero
theory_blocks.body: Two traps are easy to fall into together: assuming that a detector will read zero with no sample present, and assuming that every click once a sample arrives must come from that sample. Neither is correct. [[blue:A detector almost always registers some background clicks with no sample at all, and it keeps registering roughly that same background rate even once a sample is introduced]] - the sample's clicks simply add on top of it.

keywords.definition: Radiation energetic enough to remove electrons from atoms, creating ions.
Ionising radiation from natural and everyday sources, present even without a radioactive sample being studied.
A device, such as a Geiger-Muller tube, that registers individual ionising events.
A device connected to a detector that adds up the number of ionising events recorded, as counts.
The number of counts divided by the time interval over which they were recorded.

worked_examples.statement: **A simple count rate.** A Geiger counter records 30 counts in 10 s. Find the count rate in counts per second.
reasoning: Count rate is counts divided by the time interval over which they were recorded.
worked_examples.solution: $30\div10=3$ counts per second.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $3\,\text{counts/s}\times10\,\text{s}=30$ counts, matching the original reading.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reporting '30 counts per second' by leaving the time interval out of the calculation entirely.

worked_examples.statement: **Converting units of count rate.** A counter records 900 counts over 3 minutes. Find the count rate in counts per minute, then in counts per second.
reasoning: Find counts per minute directly by dividing by the number of minutes.
Convert minutes to seconds (3 min $=180$ s) to find counts per second.
worked_examples.solution: $900\div3=300$ counts per minute; $900\div180=5$ counts per second.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $300\,\text{counts/min}\times3\,\text{min}=900$ counts, and $5\,\text{counts/s}\times180\,\text{s}=900$ counts - both recover the original reading.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing 900 by 3 to get counts per second, forgetting that the 3 was minutes rather than seconds.

worked_examples.statement: **Isolating the sample's count rate.** With no sample present, a detector records a background count rate of 15 counts per minute. With a sample present, at the same distance and over an equal time, it records 95 counts per minute. Find the count rate due to the sample alone, and explain why 95 counts per minute is not itself the answer.
knowns: with sample $=95$ counts/min, same distance and time
unknowns: count rate due to the sample alone
reasoning: The 95 counts/min reading already includes the background that was there before the sample arrived.
Subtract the background count rate from the with-sample count rate to isolate the sample's own contribution.
worked_examples.solution: $95-15=80$ counts per minute due to the sample alone.
worked_examples.interpretation: 95 counts/min cannot be 'the sample's count rate', because background radiation (15 counts/min) is still being recorded exactly as it was before the sample was introduced; it has to be subtracted out first.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Quoting 95 counts/min directly as the sample's count rate, without subtracting the background.

worked_examples.statement: **A full background-correction calculation.** A student records 180 counts in 60 s with a sample present, and 60 counts in 60 s with no sample present, at the same distance. Calculate (a) the count rate with the sample present, (b) the background count rate, (c) the count rate due to the sample alone.
knowns: background: 60 counts in 60 s, same distance
unknowns: count rate with sample, background count rate, sample-only count rate
reasoning: Convert each count to a rate by dividing by its time interval.
Subtract the background rate from the with-sample rate to isolate the sample's own contribution.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $180\div60=3$ counts/s. (b) $60\div60=1$ count/s. (c) $3-1=2$ counts/s due to the sample alone.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $1\,\text{count/s}+2\,\text{counts/s}=3\,\text{counts/s}$, which matches the measured with-sample rate.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Giving 3 counts/s as the final answer for part (c), without subtracting the background rate found in part (b).

guided_exercises.statement: A detector records 150 counts in 50 s with a sample present. Find the count rate in counts per second.
hints: Identify the total count and the time interval separately.
Divide the count by the time interval to get the rate.
Check by multiplying your rate back by the time interval.
common_errors: Dividing 50 by 150 instead of 150 by 50, giving a rate smaller than one.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify the total count and the time interval separately.

**Step 2 — Method:** Divide the count by the time interval to get the rate.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $150\div50=3$ counts per second. Check: $3\times50=150$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check by multiplying your rate back by the time interval.

guided_exercises.statement: A background count rate of 2 counts per second is measured. With a sample present, at the same distance and for the same time, the count rate is 9 counts per second. Find the count rate due to the sample alone.
hints: Decide which of the two readings already includes the background.
Subtract the background rate from the with-sample rate.
State your answer with the correct units attached.
guided_exercises.answer: $9-2=7$ counts per second due to the sample alone.
common_errors: Adding the two rates together (giving 11) instead of subtracting one from the other.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Decide which of the two readings already includes the background.

**Step 2 — Method:** Subtract the background rate from the with-sample rate.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $9-2=7$ counts per second due to the sample alone.

**Step 4 — Check:** State your answer with the correct units attached.

exercises.statement: A counter records 240 counts in 2 minutes. Find the count rate in counts per minute, and in counts per second.
exercises.answer: $240\div2=120$ counts per minute; $120\div60=2$ counts per second.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $2\,\text{counts/s}\times120\,\text{s}=240$ counts.

exercises.statement: A sample gives a count rate of 14 counts per second, measured alongside a background count rate of 2 counts per second at the same distance. Find the count rate due to the sample alone.
exercises.answer: $14-2=12$ counts per second.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $2+12=14$, matching the original with-sample reading.

exercises.statement: With no radioactive sample present, a detector records 90 counts in one 30 s interval and 96 counts in a second, separate 30 s interval. Explain why these two background readings are not identical, even though no sample was present for either of them.
exercises.answer: Background radiation comes mostly from radioactive decay, which happens at random, so the exact number of counts in any fixed time interval varies a little from one measurement to the next, even with nothing deliberately added; 90 and 96 counts are simply two samples of this same underlying random background rate, not evidence that anything changed.
exercises.full_solution: Converting both to rates ($90\div30=3$ and $96\div30=3.2$ counts/s) shows they are close, consistent with random fluctuation around the same background level rather than a real change.

exercises.statement: A technician checking a room for a faint, possibly leaking radioactive source hears a Geiger counter clicking steadily even before testing begins. Explain why simply listening for 'any clicks at all' would not tell the technician whether a leak is present, and describe what they should measure instead.
exercises.answer: Clicks alone are not useful, because background radiation means a counter clicks even with no leak present; the technician must first measure the background count rate with no suspected source nearby, then measure the count rate at the suspect location under the same conditions, and compare the two - only a count rate clearly above background would indicate a genuine source.
exercises.full_solution: This is the same logic as isolating a sample's count rate: a reading only has meaning once it is compared against a properly measured background.

exam_questions.statement: (a) Define background radiation. (b) State two possible sources of background radiation. (c) A detector records 210 counts in 70 s. Calculate the count rate in counts per second.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Background radiation is the ionising radiation detected from natural and everyday sources, present even without a radioactive sample being deliberately studied. (b) Any two of: radon gas, rocks/building materials, cosmic rays, food and drink, medical or industrial sources. (c) $210\div70=3$ counts per second.
mark_scheme: Correct definition of background radiation.
Names one valid source of background radiation.
Names a second, different valid source.
Correctly calculates $210\div70=3$ counts per second with units.
common_errors: Naming a radioactive sample brought in deliberately as a 'source of background radiation', which misses the point that background is present regardless of any sample.

exam_questions.statement: A student wants to measure the count rate due to a radioactive sample alone. (a) Describe the two measurements they must take. (b) The background count rate is 5 counts/s; with the sample present, under the same conditions, the count rate is 23 counts/s. Calculate the count rate due to the sample alone. (c) State why the measuring distance and the counting time must be the same for both measurements.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Measure the count rate with no sample present (background), and measure the count rate with the sample present, both at the same distance and for the same length of time. (b) $23-5=18$ counts/s. (c) Changing the distance would change the count rate for reasons unconnected to the sample; using the same counting time means the two raw counts can be compared (and subtracted) directly, without first converting each one to a count rate.
exam_questions.full_solution: Check for (b): $5+18=23$, matching the with-sample reading.
mark_scheme: Describes the background-only measurement.
Describes the with-sample measurement under matching conditions.
Correctly subtracts: $23-5=18$ counts/s.
States that distance must be kept the same.
States that the same counting time lets the raw counts be compared directly (or that counts over different times must first be converted to count rates).
common_errors: Quoting 23 counts/s as the final answer to part (b), without subtracting the background.

Two counts can only be compared directly if they were measured over equal time intervals.

common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that background radiation is present from natural sources everywhere; expect a small nonzero reading before any sample is introduced.

summary.big_idea: A detector and counter measure ionising events as a count rate, but that reading always includes background radiation, which must be measured separately and subtracted to find what a sample alone is contributing.
key_points: Ionising radiation removes electrons from atoms; a detector registers each such event as a count.
Background radiation, from sources such as radon, rocks, cosmic rays and food, is present everywhere, so a detector reads above zero even with no sample present.
Count rate is counts divided by the time interval; always state the time unit.
The count rate due to a sample alone is found by subtracting a background count rate, measured at the same distance and over an equal time.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A detector's reading with a sample present is background plus sample; subtract a fairly measured background to isolate the sample's own count rate.

03_Alpha_beta_and_gamma.json.title: Alpha, beta and gamma
03_Alpha_beta_and_gamma.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Identify alpha, beta-minus and gamma radiation by their nature, relative ionising ability and penetrating power, and use these properties to predict which materials will absorb each type.

prerequisites.statement: State that the nucleus is the tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, built from protons and neutrons.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Alpha and beta radiation are both pieces of a nucleus in motion, so their charge and mass only make sense once the nucleus's own structure is already known.

prerequisites.statement: Explain that ionising radiation removes electrons from atoms, and that a detector/counter measures this as a count rate.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Identifying an emission from absorber evidence means reading and comparing count rates, exactly as practised in the previous lesson.

theory_blocks.title: Three very different things, all called 'radiation'
theory_blocks.body: An unstable nucleus can emit radiation in three distinct forms. Although all three are grouped together as 'nuclear radiation', they differ completely in what they actually are, how strongly they ionise the matter they pass through, and how far they can travel before being absorbed. [[red:Treating 'radiation' as one single thing, rather than three genuinely different emissions]], is the single biggest source of confusion in this topic.

theory_blocks.title: Nature, charge and relative mass of each type
theory_blocks.body:
- **Alpha ($\alpha$)**: a helium nucleus, made of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, with relative charge $+2$. It is relatively heavy and slow compared with the other two.
- **Beta-minus ($\beta^-$)**: a fast-moving electron, with relative charge $-1$, created inside the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton (covered fully in the next lesson). It is thousands of times lighter than an alpha particle. In this course, 'beta' always means beta-minus.
- **Gamma ($\gamma$)**: electromagnetic radiation - a high-energy photon, with no charge and no mass at all. Although it is emitted by the nucleus, it is not a particle of matter in the way alpha and beta are; it is pure electromagnetic energy.

theory_blocks.title: Ionising ability and penetrating power
theory_blocks.body:
- **Alpha** is strongly ionising (its relatively large mass and charge interact readily with nearby atoms) but weakly penetrating: it is stopped by a single sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.
- **Beta-minus** is intermediate: moderately ionising, and stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
- **Gamma** is weakly ionising (it interacts with matter far less often) but highly penetrating: it is never fully stopped, only significantly reduced, even by several centimetres of lead or thick concrete.

Ionising ability and penetrating power move in opposite directions here: the type that interacts most often with the matter around it (alpha) loses its energy, and is absorbed, the soonest.

assets.caption: Alpha is stopped by paper; beta is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma passes through both and is only greatly reduced, never fully stopped, by thick lead.
assets.purpose: Show the relative penetrating power of the three emission types through the same set of materials, in order of increasing ability to pass through matter.

theory_blocks.title: Reading absorber evidence to identify an emission
Weak penetration does not mean 'always safe'
theory_blocks.body: It is tempting to call alpha 'the safe one', since it is stopped by something as thin as paper, and to assume gamma is 'the dangerous one' because it travels furthest. From outside the body, that ranking is broadly right. But [[red:alpha's strong ionising ability makes it especially damaging if the source gets **inside** the body]] (for example, swallowed or inhaled), where there is no longer any paper or skin to stop it before it reaches living cells. Penetrating power through external materials is not the same question as overall risk, which also depends on how and where exposure happens - an idea developed further when safe use is covered.

keywords.definition: A helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons) emitted from an unstable nucleus, strongly ionising and stopped by paper.
A fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus, moderately ionising and stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
Electromagnetic radiation with no mass and no charge, weakly ionising and only reduced, never fully stopped, by thick lead or concrete.
The removal of electrons from atoms by radiation, creating ions.
How far a type of radiation can travel through matter before being absorbed.
Material placed in the path of radiation to reduce or stop it, chosen according to the type of radiation present.

worked_examples.statement: **Identifying from a description.** A nucleus emits a small, relatively heavy particle with relative charge $+2$. Identify this emission.
reasoning: Relative charge $+2$ and a heavier mass match a helium nucleus, not an electron or a photon.
worked_examples.solution: This is an **alpha particle**.
worked_examples.interpretation: Gamma has no charge at all, and beta-minus has charge $-1$, so $+2$ immediately rules both of those out.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Confusing the $+2$ charge with beta, which is negatively charged.

worked_examples.statement: **Stopped by paper.** A source's radiation is almost completely stopped by a single sheet of paper. Identify the emission type and explain your reasoning using both ionising ability and penetration.
knowns: stopped by a single sheet of paper
reasoning: Of the three types, only alpha is weakly penetrating enough to be stopped by something as thin as paper.
This fits with alpha's strong ionising ability: it loses its energy, and so is absorbed, over a very short distance.
worked_examples.solution: This is **alpha radiation**.
worked_examples.interpretation: Beta would pass through paper and need a few millimetres of aluminium to be stopped; gamma would pass through paper almost unaffected.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Identifying the emission from penetration alone, without connecting it to the matching ionising-ability reasoning.

worked_examples.statement: **Using count-rate evidence.** With no absorber, a source gives 240 counts/min. With a sheet of paper in place, the count rate drops to 14 counts/min. Identify the emission type and justify your answer numerically.
reasoning: Find the fractional drop caused by the paper: $(240-14)\div240$.
A very large drop at the paper stage (rather than a small one) points to the type that paper alone can stop.
worked_examples.solution: The drop is $(240-14)\div240\approx0.94$, a 94% reduction. This large a drop from paper alone is consistent only with **alpha radiation**.
worked_examples.interpretation: Beta or gamma would show little change at the paper stage; only alpha is absorbed almost entirely by something this thin.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Noticing that the count rate dropped at all, and concluding 'beta or gamma', without checking how large the drop actually was.

worked_examples.statement: **Two-stage absorber evidence.** A source's count rate passes through a sheet of aluminium (a few mm thick) almost unaffected, but is significantly reduced by several centimetres of thick lead (though never falling all the way to the background rate). Identify the emission and justify your answer using both results.
knowns: reduced, but not stopped, by thick lead
reasoning: Passing through aluminium almost unaffected rules out both alpha (stopped by paper, let alone aluminium) and beta (stopped by a few mm of aluminium).
Being reduced, but never fully stopped, even by thick lead is the characteristic signature of gamma radiation.
worked_examples.solution: This is **gamma radiation**.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both pieces of evidence point the same way: gamma is the only type penetrating enough to get through aluminium largely unaffected, and the only type that thick lead reduces rather than stops completely.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating 'reduced by lead' as proof of being stopped completely, when gamma is never fully absorbed by any realistic thickness.

guided_exercises.statement: A source's radiation passes through paper and through a few millimetres of aluminium almost unchanged. Its count rate falls from 300 counts/min with no absorber to 40 counts/min behind several centimetres of thick lead. Identify the emission type and justify your answer.
hints: Check what happens at the paper and aluminium stages first.
A type passing through both of those almost unaffected rules out alpha and beta.
Check whether the lead result stops the radiation completely or only reduces it.
guided_exercises.answer: This is gamma radiation: it passes through paper and aluminium largely unaffected (ruling out alpha and beta), and even thick lead only reduces its count rate from 300 to 40 counts/min rather than stopping it completely.
common_errors: Concluding 'beta', because thick lead did reduce the count rate noticeably, without checking that beta would already have been stopped at the aluminium stage.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Check what happens at the paper and aluminium stages first.

**Step 2 — Method:** A type passing through both of those almost unaffected rules out alpha and beta.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** This is gamma radiation: it passes through paper and aluminium largely unaffected (ruling out alpha and beta), and even thick lead only reduces its count rate from 300 to 40 counts/min rather than stopping it completely.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check whether the lead result stops the radiation completely or only reduces it.

guided_exercises.statement: Explain, in terms of ionising ability, why alpha radiation can be more dangerous than gamma radiation if its source gets inside the body, even though gamma travels much further outside the body.
hints: Think about what 'strongly ionising' actually means for living cells nearby.
Outside the body, skin or a short air gap already stops alpha before it reaches living tissue.
Inside the body, there is no longer anything to stop alpha before it reaches cells directly.
guided_exercises.answer: Alpha ionises far more strongly, per unit path length, than gamma does. Outside the body, this barely matters because alpha is stopped by skin or a short distance of air before it reaches living cells. Once a source is inside the body, however, alpha's intense, short-range ionisation is delivered directly to nearby cells with nothing left to stop it, making it more damaging there than gamma's weaker, more spread-out ionisation.
common_errors: Concluding that gamma must always be 'more dangerous' because it travels further, without considering where the exposure is actually happening.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Think about what 'strongly ionising' actually means for living cells nearby.

**Step 2 — Method:** Outside the body, skin or a short air gap already stops alpha before it reaches living tissue.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Alpha ionises far more strongly, per unit path length, than gamma does. Outside the body, this barely matters because alpha is stopped by skin or a short distance of air before it reaches living cells. Once a source is inside the body, however, alpha's intense, short-range ionisation is delivered directly to nearby cells with nothing left to stop it, making it more damaging there than gamma's weaker, more spread-out ionisation.

**Step 4 — Check:** Inside the body, there is no longer anything to stop alpha before it reaches cells directly.

exercises.statement: Rank alpha, beta and gamma radiation (a) from strongest to weakest ionising ability, and (b) from least to most penetrating.
exercises.answer: (a) Ionising ability, strongest to weakest: alpha, beta, gamma. (b) Penetrating power, least to most: alpha, beta, gamma.
exercises.full_solution: The two rankings run in opposite directions: the type that ionises most strongly (alpha) is stopped soonest, and so penetrates least.

exercises.statement: A source gives 150 counts/min with no absorber, 145 counts/min with paper in place, and 12 counts/min with a few millimetres of aluminium in place. Identify the emission type and justify your answer with both results.
exercises.answer: This is beta radiation: paper barely changes the count rate (150 to 145 counts/min), ruling out alpha, but a few millimetres of aluminium reduces it almost to nothing (145 to 12 counts/min), which is beta's characteristic absorption thickness.
exercises.full_solution: Paper causes only a $(150-145)\div150\approx3\%$ drop, while aluminium causes a further $(145-12)\div145\approx92\%$ drop - a small drop then a large one, matching beta.

exercises.statement: Explain why gamma radiation, despite being the weakest ioniser of the three types, can still be dangerous with prolonged exposure or at high enough intensity.
exercises.answer: Although gamma ionises weakly per interaction, it penetrates almost everything, including the whole body, and can reach every cell it passes through; over a long exposure, or at high enough intensity, these many weak interactions add up to a damaging total dose, even without any single interaction being especially strong.
exercises.full_solution: Although gamma ionises weakly per interaction, it penetrates almost everything, including the whole body, and can reach every cell it passes through; over a long exposure, or at high enough intensity, these many weak interactions add up to a damaging total dose, even without any single interaction being especially strong.

exercises.statement: A technician investigating an unknown source measures: no absorber, 220 counts/min; with paper, 210 counts/min; with 5 mm of aluminium, 8 counts/min. Identify the emission type, explaining your reasoning step by step using both results.
exercises.answer: This is beta radiation. Paper barely changes the reading (220 to 210 counts/min, about a 4.5% drop), which rules out alpha, since alpha would have been almost completely stopped by paper alone. Aluminium then causes a large drop (210 to 8 counts/min, about a 96% drop), which is the absorption behaviour expected of beta, not gamma, which would still pass through a few millimetres of aluminium largely unaffected.
exercises.full_solution: Both pieces of evidence agree: a small drop at paper followed by a large drop at aluminium is the beta signature; it would take a large drop at paper (alpha) or only a partial drop even behind thick lead (gamma) to point elsewhere.

exam_questions.statement: (a) State the nature of an alpha particle and of a gamma ray. (b) Using the words 'ionising' and 'penetrating', describe the key difference between them. (c) State one material that would significantly reduce gamma radiation.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Alpha is a helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons); gamma is electromagnetic radiation, with no mass and no charge. (b) Alpha is strongly ionising but weakly penetrating (stopped by paper); gamma is weakly ionising but highly penetrating (never fully stopped). (c) Thick lead (or thick concrete).

exam_questions.statement: A student tests an unknown source: no absorber, 280 counts/min; with paper, 35 counts/min; with 3 mm of aluminium, 30 counts/min. (a) Identify the emission type. (b) Justify your answer using the data given. (c) State what you would expect to happen if a thick sheet of lead were used instead of aluminium.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Alpha radiation. (b) Paper alone causes a very large drop (280 to 35 counts/min, about an 87.5% reduction), which only alpha is weak enough in penetration to show; the alpha particles have already been stopped by the paper, so the remaining 30 to 35 counts/min is mostly background radiation; the tiny further change with aluminium (35 to 30 counts/min) is within normal random variation, not a separate absorption stage. (c) With the alpha radiation already stopped by the paper and aluminium, a thick lead sheet would make little further difference to the count rate.
exam_questions.full_solution: The key evidence is the size of the first drop: an 87.5% reduction from paper alone is far larger than beta or gamma would produce, and points directly to alpha.
mark_scheme: Correctly identifies alpha.
Calculates or correctly estimates the large percentage drop caused by paper.
Explains that this large a drop from paper alone is alpha's characteristic behaviour.
Explains the small further change with aluminium as consistent with the alpha already having been stopped by the paper (the remaining count rate being mainly background).
Correctly predicts little further change with thick lead, since the emission is already almost entirely stopped.
common_errors: Identifying beta because aluminium caused some further reduction, without recognising that the dominant drop had already happened at the paper stage.

flashcards.front: What three types of nuclear radiation does this course cover?
flashcards.back: Alpha, beta (beta-minus) and gamma.

flashcards.front: What is alpha radiation?
flashcards.back: A helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons), emitted from an unstable nucleus, with relative charge $+2$.

flashcards.front: Why does alpha radiation ionise so strongly but travel such a short distance?
flashcards.back: Its relatively large mass and charge make it interact very readily with nearby atoms, transferring its energy, and so being absorbed, over a very short range.

flashcards.front: Is gamma radiation a particle with mass, like alpha and beta?
flashcards.back: No. Gamma is electromagnetic radiation: it has no mass and no charge at all.

flashcards.front: Rank alpha, beta and gamma from most to least ionising, and then from least to most penetrating.
flashcards.back: Most to least ionising: alpha, beta, gamma. Least to most penetrating: alpha, beta, gamma.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Gamma radiation is a particle with mass, like alpha.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Alpha, beta and gamma are taught together as a set of three emissions, and it is easy to assume they are all 'the same kind of thing', just with different masses.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: A learner describes gamma radiation as 'a small particle' or assigns it a charge or a mass.
misconceptions.correct_model: Gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation - a high-energy photon with no mass and no charge - unlike alpha and beta, which are genuine particles ejected from the nucleus.
misconceptions.remediation: List the three emissions with their nature side by side: alpha (a helium nucleus), beta-minus (an electron), gamma (electromagnetic radiation, not a particle at all) - make the odd one out explicit.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Whichever type of radiation penetrates furthest must also ionise most strongly wherever it goes.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 'Strongest' and 'furthest' both sound like ways of saying a radiation type is 'more powerful', so they are easy to lump together.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: A learner assumes gamma is 'the most dangerous' simply because it travels furthest, without separating ionising ability from range.
misconceptions.correct_model: Penetration and ionising ability trade off in the opposite direction: alpha ionises most strongly per unit path but is stopped almost immediately (shortest range); gamma ionises most weakly per interaction but travels furthest (longest range), precisely because it interacts with matter so much less often.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast the two properties directly using the absorber evidence: the type stopped soonest (alpha) is the one that interacts, and therefore ionises, most intensely along its short path.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Beta radiation could just as well mean a positively charged particle (beta-plus), so its charge is ambiguous.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A positive form of beta decay (beta-plus) does exist in physics more broadly, so without a clear scope statement, 'beta' can seem to leave the charge open.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: A learner is unsure whether to give beta a positive or a negative charge, or assumes 'beta' alone fixes nothing about sign.
misconceptions.correct_model: In this course, 'beta radiation' always means beta-minus: a fast-moving electron, with negative charge, created when a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton. A positive form (beta-plus) exists in physics but is outside this course's scope.
misconceptions.remediation: State explicitly, every time beta is introduced, that it means beta-minus here, and give it a definite negative charge and small mass (much smaller than alpha's) without hedging.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating gamma as a particle with mass and charge.
common_mistakes.why: Gamma is usually listed alongside alpha and beta, which are genuine particles, making it easy to assume gamma is too.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember gamma is electromagnetic radiation, not matter at all - give it no mass and no charge every time.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming the furthest-penetrating type must also ionise most strongly.
common_mistakes.why: Both 'ionises strongly' and 'penetrates far' sound like ways of describing a 'more powerful' radiation.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember the trade-off: strong ionisation uses up a particle's energy quickly, over a short range, so the strongest ioniser (alpha) is also the least penetrating.

common_mistakes.why: Alpha is stopped by paper, which sounds completely harmless.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask where the exposure is happening: alpha's strong ionisation makes it dangerous specifically if the source gets inside the body, where nothing is left to stop it.

exam_notes: Always give two pieces of evidence (what passed through, what was absorbed) when identifying an emission type from an experiment, not just one.
State ionising ability and penetrating power as two separate properties - never conflate 'penetrates far' with 'ionises strongly'.
Remember that weak penetration does not mean harmless, especially if a source could get inside the body; this links directly to safe-use precautions.

summary.big_idea: Alpha, beta and gamma differ completely in nature, and their ionising ability and penetrating power trade off in opposite directions: the strongest ioniser (alpha) is stopped soonest, and the weakest ioniser (gamma) travels furthest.
key_points: Alpha is a helium nucleus (charge $+2$); beta-minus is a fast electron (charge $-1$); gamma is electromagnetic radiation (no mass, no charge).
Alpha: strongly ionising, stopped by paper. Beta: intermediate, stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Gamma: weakly ionising, only reduced (never fully stopped) by thick lead.
An emission type can be identified from how its count rate changes behind successive absorbers, using fair, equal-distance and equal-time comparisons.
Weak penetration does not mean harmless: alpha is especially damaging if its source is inside the body.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Alpha ionises strongest and penetrates least; gamma ionises weakest and penetrates most; beta sits in between on both counts.

04_Random_decay_and_half-life.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Explain that radioactive decay of individual nuclei is random and spontaneous, that decay changes which element is present, and that in beta-minus emission a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron.
Complete and balance alpha, beta-minus and gamma nuclide equations using conservation of nucleon number (A) and proton number (Z).
Read a half-life from a decay table or decay curve, and calculate the activity or count rate remaining after a whole number of half-lives.

prerequisites.statement: State the meaning of proton number (Z) and nucleon number (A), and calculate neutrons as $A-Z$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Balancing a decay equation is exactly a check that the total $A$ and the total $Z$ match on both sides, using the same counts first defined in an earlier lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Describe alpha, beta-minus and gamma radiation by their nature and relative penetration.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Each decay equation emits one of these three, so knowing what is physically being emitted (a helium nucleus, an electron, or a photon) makes sense of why $A$ and $Z$ change the way they do.

prerequisites.statement: Read a value from a graph's axes and identify a repeated pattern in a table of data.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A decay curve is read by finding where the activity has halved, which depends entirely on reading values off two axes and spotting the repeating halving pattern.

theory_blocks.title: Random for one nucleus, predictable for billions
theory_blocks.body:
**Radioactive decay** is a change in an unstable nucleus that results in the emission of an alpha particle or a beta particle and/or gamma radiation. It is **spontaneous**: it happens on its own, and heating, compressing or chemically reacting the material does not speed it up or slow it down. It is also **random**: whether, and exactly when, any single unstable nucleus decays cannot be predicted at all: nothing about its past, and nothing you could measure about it, lets you predict the moment it will decay. This is genuinely different from everyday randomness like a die roll, where in principle more information could improve a prediction - a nucleus's decay time cannot be predicted even in principle.

Yet a sample containing billions of identical unstable nuclei behaves in a completely predictable way as a whole: on average, half of however many nuclei are present right now will have decayed after one [[blue:**half-life**]], whatever that half-life happens to be. This is the same pattern that makes a huge number of random coin flips land close to half heads, even though no individual flip can be predicted. Randomness at the level of one nucleus and predictability at the level of a large population are not a contradiction - they are two different, equally true, descriptions of the same process, one of the most important ideas in this entire topic.

theory_blocks.title: Which element you get after each type of decay
theory_blocks.body:
Alpha and beta decay always change the nucleus into that of a different element, because they change its proton number; gamma emission does not:

- **Alpha decay**: the nucleon number falls by 4 and the proton number falls by 2 (a helium nucleus, $^4_2\mathrm{He}$, is emitted). The new element is two places earlier in the periodic table.
- **Beta-minus decay**: the nucleon number stays the same and the proton number rises by 1 (an electron is emitted). The new element is one place later in the periodic table.
- **Gamma emission**: neither the nucleon number nor the proton number changes. The nucleus is still the same nuclide, simply with less energy than before.

A change of element is the clearest sign that alpha or beta decay - not gamma emission alone - has taken place.

theory_blocks.title: Half-life: the time for half of a sample to decay
theory_blocks.body:
The **half-life** of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for half of the unstable nuclei present, at any chosen starting moment, to decay. Equivalently, since activity (or a measured count rate, under fixed geometry) is proportional to how many unstable nuclei remain, the half-life is also the time for the activity or count rate to fall to half its previous value.

For a sample with an initial count rate of $80$ counts/min and a half-life of $5$ minutes: after one half-life (5 min), the count rate is $80\div2=40$ counts/min; after two half-lives (10 min), it is $40\div2=20$ counts/min. Each half-life halves whatever value was present at the start of that half-life - not the original starting value.

assets.caption: A decay curve for a sample with half-life 5 minutes and initial count rate 80 counts/min: the count rate halves (to 40, then to 20 counts/min) over each successive 5-minute half-life, marked with dashed guide lines.
assets.purpose: Show the halving pattern of a decay curve with clearly spaced, numerically verified half-life points, so half-life can be read directly off a graph rather than only from a table.

theory_blocks.title: Writing and balancing a nuclide equation
theory_blocks.body:
A decay can be written as a nuclide equation, with the parent nucleus on the left and the daughter nucleus plus the emitted particle on the right. The nucleon numbers must add up to the same total on both sides, and so must the proton numbers - nothing is created or destroyed, only rearranged.

**Alpha decay:** $^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow\ ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$

For uranium-238 ($Z=92$): $^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}\rightarrow\ ^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$. Check nucleon numbers: $234+4=238$. Check proton numbers: $90+2=92$.

**Beta-minus decay:** $^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow\ ^{A}_{Z+1}Y + {}^{0}_{-1}e$

For carbon-14 ($Z=6$): $^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}\rightarrow\ ^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}e$. Check nucleon numbers: $14+0=14$. Check proton numbers: $7+(-1)=6$.

**Gamma emission** (from an already-formed excited nucleus): $^{A}_{Z}X^{*} \rightarrow\ ^{A}_{Z}X + \gamma$, with $A$ and $Z$ unchanged on both sides.

theory_blocks.title: Why beta-minus decay happens: a neutron becomes a proton
theory_blocks.body: Beta-minus decay happens because, inside the nucleus, a neutron spontaneously changes into a proton, with a fast-moving electron released as the beta particle. This explains exactly the pattern seen above: [[blue:a neutron turning into a proton leaves the total number of nucleons unchanged (a neutron is simply replaced by a proton), while the proton number rises by exactly 1.]] No proton is destroyed and no new nucleon appears from nowhere - one type of nucleon is converted into the other.

keywords.definition: The unpredictable decay of an individual unstable nucleus, with no way to know in advance when it will decay.
The time taken for half of the unstable nuclei present in a sample, at a given moment, to decay.
The rate at which unstable nuclei in a sample decay, measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq is one decay per second; often followed via a detector's count rate under fixed geometry.
An equation showing a parent nuclide decaying into a daughter nuclide plus an emitted particle, with nucleon number and proton number conserved.
Decay in which a nucleus emits a helium nucleus, reducing its nucleon number by 4 and its proton number by 2.
Decay in which a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton, emitting an electron; nucleon number is unchanged, proton number rises by 1.
The release of electromagnetic radiation from a nucleus, changing neither its nucleon number nor its proton number.

worked_examples.statement: **Two half-lives.** A sample has an initial count rate of 80 counts/min and a half-life of 5 minutes. Find the count rate after 1 half-life and after 2 half-lives.
reasoning: Each half-life halves the value present at its start.
Apply the halving twice in a row, once for each half-life that passes.
worked_examples.solution: After 1 half-life (5 min): $80\div2=40$ counts/min. After 2 half-lives (10 min): $40\div2=20$ counts/min.
worked_examples.interpretation: The sample never reaches zero: after two half-lives, a nonzero count rate of 20 counts/min remains, exactly a quarter of the original value.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Halving the original value twice separately and then adding the results, instead of repeatedly halving what remains.

worked_examples.statement: **Completing an alpha-decay equation.** Uranium-238 ($Z=92$) decays by emitting an alpha particle. Write the equation, identify the daughter nuclide (thorium, symbol Th), and check it balances.
unknowns: daughter nucleon number and proton number
reasoning: Alpha decay reduces the nucleon number by 4 and the proton number by 2.
Subtract these from the parent's values to find the daughter.
worked_examples.solution: Daughter: $A=238-4=234$, $Z=92-2=90$, giving $^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$. Equation: $^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}\rightarrow\ ^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: nucleon numbers $234+4=238$; proton numbers $90+2=92$ - both sides balance.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Subtracting only from $A$ (or only from $Z$) and leaving the other number unchanged on the daughter.

worked_examples.statement: **Beta-minus decay of carbon-14.** Carbon-14 ($Z=6$) decays by beta-minus emission. Write the equation, identify the daughter nuclide (nitrogen, symbol N), and explain why the nucleon number does not change even though the proton number does.
unknowns: daughter nucleon number and proton number
reasoning: Beta-minus decay keeps the nucleon number the same and raises the proton number by 1.

This matches a neutron inside the nucleus changing into a proton: one nucleon is replaced by another, so the total nucleon count is unaffected, but a neutron (contributing 0 to $Z$) becomes a proton (contributing 1 to $Z$).
worked_examples.solution: Daughter: $A=14$ (unchanged), $Z=6+1=7$, giving $^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N}$. Equation: $^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}\rightarrow\ ^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}e$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: nucleon numbers $14+0=14$; proton numbers $7+(-1)=6$ - both sides balance.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reducing the nucleon number by 1, mistakenly treating the emitted electron as if it were a full nucleon leaving the nucleus.

worked_examples.statement: **Half-life over several days.** Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A sample starts with an activity of 160 Bq. Find its activity after 24 days.
reasoning: Find the number of half-lives elapsed: $24\div8=3$.
Halve the activity once for each half-life, three times in total.
worked_examples.solution: $160\to80\to40\to20$ Bq, so the activity after 24 days is $20$ Bq.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $160\div2^3=160\div8=20$, matching the repeated-halving result.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing 160 by 24 directly, instead of first converting 24 days into a whole number of half-lives.

worked_examples.statement: **Working backwards from a ratio.** A sample's count rate falls from 240 counts/min to 15 counts/min while measured at the same distance and for the same time throughout. Its half-life is 2 hours. Find how long this fall took, by repeatedly halving 240 until you reach 15.
reasoning: Halve 240 repeatedly, counting how many halvings are needed to reach 15: $240\to120\to60\to30\to15$.
That took 4 halvings, so 4 half-lives have passed; multiply by the half-life to get the elapsed time.
worked_examples.solution: 4 half-lives $\times\,2$ h $=8$ h.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $240\div2^4=240\div16=15$, confirming 4 half-lives is correct.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing 240 by 15 to get 16 and using that number directly as the number of half-lives, instead of recognising that 16 is $2^4$, meaning 4 half-lives.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading a half-life from a decay curve.** The graph shows how the activity of a radioactive sample changes with time. Use the graph to find the half-life of the isotope, then calculate the activity of the sample after 24 hours.
knowns: the decay curve of activity (Bq) against time (hours)
unknowns: the half-life, read from the curve
reasoning: Read the starting activity off the curve at $t=0$, then halve it.
Read off the time at which the curve reaches that halved value: that time is the half-life.
Find how many half-lives fit into 24 hours, then halve the starting activity once for each of them.
worked_examples.solution: At $t=0$ the curve starts at $80$ Bq, so half of this is $40$ Bq. The curve passes through $40$ Bq at $t=6$ h, so the half-life is $6$ hours. In 24 hours, $24\div6=4$ half-lives pass, so the activity halves four times: $80\to40\to20\to10\to5$, giving $5$ Bq after 24 hours.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $80\div2^4=80\div16=5$ Bq, and the curve does indeed pass close to $5$ Bq at the right-hand edge of the graph. Any pair of points on the curve would give the same half-life - from $40$ Bq at 6 h to $20$ Bq at 12 h is again 6 hours.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reading the time at which the curve looks as if it has reached zero and calling that the half-life, instead of the time for the activity to fall to half its value.
